definition: Supplant means to take the place of another, often by force or scheming.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word supplant. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know supplant should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: In three winters the snowmobile supplanted the dog team across the delta, and the kennels went quiet.
Succeed is the mild, lawful end of this scale, gentler than supplant — the heir succeeds the founder with everyone's blessing and nobody pushed, while to supplant is to slip into a place uninvited.
Overthrow goes further than supplant: not a quiet slide into someone's chair but open force — the palace stormed, not whispered through.

Oust means to force someone out openly — blunt, immediate, and visible to everyone. Supplant is quieter and tells more of the story: the rival's place is taken from beneath them by patient maneuvering, and the schemer ends up holding it.

Unseat means to remove someone from an official seat or title — a champion, an incumbent — and it says nothing about who moves in next. Supplant completes the exchange: one holder is eased out, and the newcomer settles into the very place that was theirs.

Supplant means to take the place of another, often by force or scheming.
The understudy did not wait for luck: she learned the lead's blocking, courted the director at every note session, and by spring had supplanted her on the opening-night card.
Supplant is sharper than replace because it keeps the smell of the maneuver — the lead did not step down or wear out; her place was taken from beneath her, move by patient move.
Supplant tells a small story: something held a place, and something else now holds it — often after pushing.
Use it for rivals, invasive species, and technologies that shoulder predecessors aside.
Supersede, taught in this unit, is the paperwork version, an orderly succession by the newer standard; if the takeover was earned by open force, overthrow or oust says so louder.

When garden centers first sold the silver reed as an ornamental border plant, nobody imagined it would supplant the native cattails within a decade.
The reed did not storm the marsh; it crept.
Each spring its runners pushed a few feet farther beneath the mud, sprouting wherever the cattails thinned, never announcing themselves.
By the time the county surveyed the wetland, the cattails held less than a tenth of their old ground, and the reed stood in their place, row after silver row.
Ecologists know the pattern well: the takeover works not by killing anything outright, but by quietly occupying every space the older plant leaves open.
